title: Sex, Gender, and Social Construction
description: Distinguishing sex from gender and how gender is built, not born

concepts.title: Sex and Gender
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociologists draw a working distinction between sex and gender. Sex refers to biological characteristics — chromosomes, hormones, gonads, anatomy — while gender refers to the cultural meanings, norms, and identities attached to being a man, woman, or another category.

This distinction was sharpened by Ann Oakley in Sex, Gender and Society (1972), drawing on earlier work by psychiatrist Robert Stoller. The key claim: even if some sex differences are biological, the elaborate apparatus of masculinity and femininity — clothing, behaviour, occupations, expectations — is cultural and historically variable.

The distinction has limits. Anne Fausto-Sterling and others argue that biological sex itself is not strictly binary: intersex variation, hormonal continua, and developmental complexity show that even 'sex' is partly a social classification of a messier biology. Gender and sex co-constitute each other, but the conceptual split remains analytically useful.

concepts.title: Beauvoir: Becoming a Woman
concepts.contentHtml:
Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (1949) opens with the most quoted line in feminist theory: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' Beauvoir's claim is existentialist: there is no fixed feminine essence; womanhood is a situation produced through socialisation, expectation, and constraint.

Beauvoir analysed woman as the Other — defined relative to the male subject who poses as the universal human. Man is the One, woman is the Second; man acts, woman is acted upon. This asymmetry is not a natural fact but a historical structure produced by myth, religion, law, and family.

Beauvoir's existentialist framing — situation, project, freedom — anticipated the constructionist turn. Later theorists would push further, but the core insight remains: gender is something we do and undergo, not something we simply are.

concepts.title: Doing Gender
concepts.contentHtml:
Candace West and Don Zimmerman's article Doing Gender (1987) reframed gender as an ongoing accomplishment, not a property someone has. Gender is produced moment by moment in interaction: how we walk, dress, speak, occupy space, address others.

They distinguished three layers: sex (biological criteria), sex category (the social classification we are placed in at a glance), and gender (conduct that displays one as a competent member of that category). We are 'held accountable' for behaving in ways that fit our sex category — and judged when we fail.

This account is powerful because it locates gender in mundane social practice rather than in deep psychology or biology. Gender is not behind our actions; it is in them. The implication is that gender can in principle be done differently, even if institutional pressure heavily constrains the choreography.

title: Performativity and Queer Theory
description: Butler, performativity, heteronormativity, and the queer challenge

concepts.title: Butler's Performativity
concepts.contentHtml:
Judith Butler's Gender Trouble (1990) pushed constructionism to its radical conclusion. For Butler, gender is performative: it is constituted by the very acts said to express it. There is no inner gendered self that the performance reveals; the repeated performance produces the appearance of an inner self.

Butler distinguishes performativity from theatrical performance. We do not freely choose gender each morning. Rather, gendered acts are citations of prior norms, repeated under social compulsion. The illusion of natural gender comes from the sheer density and consistency of these citations across a lifetime.

Butler also attacks the heterosexual matrix: the cultural grid that demands sex, gender, and desire line up — female bodies expressing femininity desiring men, and so on. Bodies that fail this alignment are rendered unintelligible. The political pay-off: parody, drag, and queer practice can expose gender's contingency.

concepts.title: Heteronormativity and the Sex Hierarchy
concepts.contentHtml:
Michael Warner coined heteronormativity in 1991 to name the way institutions — law, medicine, family, media — treat heterosexuality as the default, natural, and morally privileged orientation. Heteronormativity is not just prejudice against gay people; it is a background structure that shapes tax codes, hospital visiting rules, school curricula, and the imagined audience of every advertisement.

Anthropologist Gayle Rubin, in Thinking Sex (1984), mapped what she called the charmed circle of socially approved sexuality: heterosexual, married, monogamous, procreative, vanilla, same-generation, in private. Outside lies the 'outer limits' — queer, casual, commercial, cross-generational — stigmatised and policed.

The sex hierarchy is enforced through criminal law, religion, psychiatric diagnosis, and informal disgust. Queer theorists argue that liberation requires not only tolerance but the dismantling of the hierarchy itself.

concepts.title: Queer Theory and Transgender Studies
concepts.contentHtml:
Queer theory, emerging from work by Eve Sedgwick, Butler, and others around 1990, refuses fixed identity categories. 'Queer' is used as a verb as much as a noun: to queer is to denaturalise, to expose the constructedness of seemingly given categories. It is suspicious of even the homo/hetero binary itself.

Sedgwick's Epistemology of the Closet (1990) argued that twentieth-century Western culture is structured by an unstable opposition between hetero- and homosexuality, with the closet as a defining institution of public/private knowledge.

Transgender studies, formalised in the 1990s with Susan Stryker and others, centres trans experience and critiques the medical and legal gatekeeping of gender. It argues that trans lives are not edge cases but reveal how gender works for everyone: the labour of becoming, the policing of categories, the productivity of self-fashioning. Queer and trans theory together pluralise the field beyond the man/woman frame.

title: Feminist Waves and Intersectionality
description: From suffrage to #MeToo, and the intersectional turn

concepts.title: First and Second Waves
concepts.contentHtml:
Historians often periodise feminist movements into waves. The first wave, roughly 1848 to 1920 in the United States and Britain, focused on legal personhood: property rights, education, divorce, and above all the vote. Key moments include Seneca Falls (1848), the suffragette campaigns of the Pankhursts, and the Nineteenth Amendment (1920).

The second wave opened in the 1960s, broadening from formal equality to the politics of everyday life. Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) named the malaise of educated suburban housewives — 'the problem that has no name' — as a political problem. The slogan 'the personal is political' captured the move from law to family, sexuality, housework, and reproduction.

Second-wave practice included consciousness-raising groups in which women examined their own experiences as data about a shared structural condition. Reproductive rights, sexual harassment, and rape law became central campaigns.

concepts.title: Intersectionality
concepts.contentHtml:
Legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw coined intersectionality in 1989 to analyse how multiple axes of oppression — gender, race, class, sexuality, disability — interact rather than add. Crenshaw was responding to anti-discrimination cases such as DeGraffenreid v. General Motors, where Black women's claims fell between race and sex categories that the law treated separately.

Intersectionality argues that the experience of a Black working-class lesbian is not the experience of a white woman plus the experience of a Black man plus the experience of a lesbian; it is something distinct, shaped by the intersection itself. Patricia Hill Collins' Black Feminist Thought (1990) gave the concept sociological depth by analysing the matrix of domination.

bell hooks had earlier insisted, in Ain't I a Woman? (1981), that mainstream feminism centred white middle-class concerns. Intersectionality reframes feminism as a project of all marginalised people, not a single-axis politics of 'women' as a homogeneous class.

concepts.title: Third and Fourth Waves
concepts.contentHtml:
The third wave, beginning in the early 1990s, embraced internal plurality and the intersectional critiques that had built up. Influenced by post-structuralism, queer theory, and women of colour feminism, it was sceptical of the universal subject 'woman'. Riot Grrrl music, sex-positive feminism, and the embrace of contradiction (femininity, makeup, sex work) marked third-wave style.

The fourth wave is generally dated to the early 2010s and is defined by digital infrastructure: hashtags, viral testimony, and networked organising. The #MeToo movement, founded by Tarana Burke in 2006 and exploding in 2017 after the Weinstein revelations, brought sexual harassment from private knowledge to public reckoning at scale.

The wave metaphor is contested — it can flatten continuity, ignore the Global South, and obscure ongoing first-wave struggles in many countries. But it captures real shifts in tactics, infrastructure, and political horizons across two centuries of organised feminism.

title: Patriarchy, Work, and the Wage Gap
description: Hegemonic masculinity, the second shift, and labour market inequality

concepts.title: Patriarchy and Hegemonic Masculinity
concepts.contentHtml:
Patriarchy in sociology names a system in which men, on average, hold disproportionate power across institutions: politics, economy, household, religion, media. Sylvia Walby's Theorizing Patriarchy (1990) identified six structures — paid work, household, the state, violence, sexuality, and culture — that together reproduce male dominance.

R. W. Connell's Masculinities (1995) refined the picture by showing that patriarchy is not uniform among men. Hegemonic masculinity is the culturally exalted form — typically associated with whiteness, heterosexuality, physical strength, emotional restraint, and economic success — that subordinates other masculinities (gay, working-class, racialised) and femininities.

The 'patriarchal dividend' is the benefit men collectively receive from this arrangement, even if most men do not embody the hegemonic ideal. Connell's framework lets us analyse gender power without flattening men into a single homogeneous oppressor class.

concepts.title: The Second Shift and Care Work
concepts.contentHtml:
Even in dual-earner households, unpaid domestic labour falls heavily on women. Arlie Hochschild's The Second Shift (1989), based on interviews with American couples, found that working women did roughly an extra month of full-time work per year on housework and childcare compared with their male partners.

Hochschild also identified emotional labour: the work of managing one's feelings to produce desired emotional states in others — central to feminised service jobs (flight attendants, nurses, receptionists) and to family life.

The motherhood penalty describes the wage and promotion losses women suffer after having children, while research by Shelley Correll and others finds a corresponding fatherhood bonus for men. Cross-national data from the OECD show that the gendered division of unpaid care, more than overt discrimination at hiring, drives much of the persistent wage gap.

concepts.title: The Wage Gap and Occupational Segregation
concepts.contentHtml:
The gross wage gap compares median earnings of women and men. In the United States in the early 2020s, women earned roughly 82 cents for every dollar earned by men in full-time work, with larger gaps for Black and Hispanic women.

The controlled gap adjusts for occupation, hours, education, and experience. It shrinks but does not vanish — leaving a residual often attributed to discrimination or unmeasured factors. Critics argue that controlling for occupation hides part of the inequality, since the channelling of women into lower-paid fields is itself a gendered outcome.

Sociologist Barbara Reskin showed that occupational segregation — nursing, teaching, and administrative work feminised; engineering, finance, and trades masculinised — accounts for a large share of the gap. The glass ceiling blocks women from top positions; the glass escalator, identified by Christine Williams, accelerates men's promotion in feminised professions.

title: Sexuality, Power, and Discourse
description: Foucault, compulsory heterosexuality, scripts, and Kinsey

concepts.title: Foucault and the Production of Sexuality
concepts.contentHtml:
Michel Foucault's History of Sexuality, Volume 1 (1976) overturned a common story. The familiar narrative — that the Victorians repressed sex and modernity gradually liberated it — Foucault calls the repressive hypothesis. He argues that the nineteenth century did not silence sex; it generated an unprecedented explosion of discourse about it: medicine, psychiatry, demography, pedagogy, the confessional, the law.

For Foucault, 'sexuality' is not a natural object that science gradually discovered, but a historically produced apparatus that organises bodies, pleasures, identities, and populations. The 'homosexual' as a kind of person, he argued, was invented in the late nineteenth century — earlier eras had sodomy as an act, not orientation as identity.

Power, in this view, is not only repressive but productive: it produces categories, identities, knowledges, and the very desires it then governs. Sexuality becomes a privileged site for modern bio-power.

concepts.title: Compulsory Heterosexuality and Scripts
concepts.contentHtml:
Adrienne Rich's Compulsory Heterosexuality and Lesbian Existence (1980) argued that heterosexuality is not a free choice but an institution actively enforced through law, economic dependence, sexual violence, media, and the erasure of lesbian history. The question is not why some women are lesbians but why so many women, given a genuine choice, would become heterosexual.

Rich introduced the lesbian continuum: a range of woman-identified experience from intimate friendship to sexual partnership, recovering bonds between women that patriarchy renders invisible.

From a different angle, John Gagnon and William Simon's sexual scripts theory (1973) treats sexual behaviour as guided by culturally available scripts at three levels: cultural scenarios (what counts as sex), interpersonal scripts (who does what with whom), and intrapsychic scripts (private fantasy). Sexuality is rehearsed and improvised within these scripts, not driven by raw biological urge.

concepts.title: Kinsey and Cross-Cultural Variation
concepts.contentHtml:
Alfred Kinsey's reports — Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953) — shocked mid-century America by documenting that masturbation, premarital sex, extramarital sex, and same-sex experience were far more common than public morality acknowledged.

Kinsey introduced the 0–6 Kinsey scale, treating sexual orientation as a continuum rather than a binary. Although his samples were not nationally representative and his methodology has been criticised, his data ended the assumption of a clean heterosexual norm with rare deviation.

Cross-cultural anthropology has further shown the variability of sexual organisation. Margaret Mead's work in Sex and Temperament (1935) described societies with very different gender temperaments. Studies of hijra in South Asia, two-spirit roles in many Indigenous North American nations, and ritualised same-sex initiation in parts of Melanesia all illustrate that the modern Western matrix of two genders and two orientations is one cultural arrangement among many.
